attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his signed 2022 essay, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Both conjuncts are kept, along with 'systems like GPT-3' and 'no matter how much experience'. The first conjunct is closer to a present-tense description. The unlimited 'never' fairly makes the combined claim a categorical forecast.

contract.note: Reading 'systems like GPT-3' as GPT-style models is ordinary. So is reading 'gravitate' as learning human language more readily than artificial controls; Marcus's own essay says they are equally at home with non-human languages. The conjunction rule (refuting either part refutes the whole) is fair. The result still depends on that reading.

evidence.note: Dated controlled study: GPT-2 learns English more easily than systematically altered languages. A preference for human language under the contract reading.
Independent 12-language follow-up (v2, May 2025) finds some human-like inductive bias. It is weaker than in humans and imperfect, but it is present, which corroborates e1.
Methodological critique: one key comparison mixes counting rules with non-adjacency. This weakens claims of human-specific constraints, but not the basic preference the contract requires.
Tested generative models show incoherent world models. Fits a present limitation but cannot establish 'never, no matter how much experience'.
Positive state-tracking results, but only in restricted text environments after targeted training. Not broad cohesive understanding, so it neither refutes nor confirms the second part.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met for the first part. Two independent controlled studies (e1, e2) find GPT-style models learn human language more readily than impossible variants, which contradicts 'do not gravitate'. The critique in e3 limits only the stronger human-specific reading. The 'never cohesive understanding' part stays unresolved (e4, e5). Under the contract's conjunction rule, the combined claim is contradicted.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed essay.

semantics.note: Fair paraphrase of the core. It drops the minor 'don't tell us why the world is as it is' clause but keeps the explanation and 'merely mimic' points.

contract.note: The contract rightly treats 'explanation' as a philosophy-of-science standard and 'merely mimic' as a contested description with no agreed measure. It does not stretch the claim either way.

evidence.note: GPT-3 paper confirms it is an autoregressive text predictor. Says nothing on explanatory value.
Copying study on GPT-2, not GPT-3: output is partly novel, partly copied. Bears loosely on 'mimic' and does not settle the claim.

reviews.rationale: The claim mixes a normative standard for scientific explanation with a contested description of what the model has learned. Neither part has an agreed measure, and the packet offers only context. It is too vague to score, so not adjudicable.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his signed essay.

semantics.note: Keeps both the effect (no capacity to avoid misinformation) and the stated cause (models word relations, not the world).

contract.note: Reading 'no capacity to avoid' as 'cannot reliably avoid' is fair and ordinary. Requiring controlled causal evidence fits the 'because' claim.

evidence.note: TruthfulQA ties GPT-3's falsehoods to imitating its training text. This partly fits the word-statistics story but does not test grounding as the missing factor.
Text-only human-feedback tuning cut hallucination from 41% to 21%. Errors fell without any world grounding but were not removed, so the effect fits while the cause stays unsettled.

reviews.rationale: The evidence fits the claim that GPT-3 could not reliably avoid falsehoods. But no study in the packet separates text-only training from other causes, and e2 shows errors falling without grounding. The causal part is not settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed essay.

semantics.note: Keeps 'essentially regurgitation' with his gloss (matching trained patterns). Also keeps that the feat does not imply knowing word meanings.

contract.note: The contract correctly notes 'regurgitation' is glossed figuratively, and that 'knows what words mean' had no agreed test. No stretched reading is imposed.

evidence.note: GPT-2 copying study gives a mixed picture of novelty and copying. It would bear only on a literal reading Marcus did not use, and it is not about GPT-3.
Same abstract: GPT-2 often makes semantic errors. Fits his doubt about meaning but does not test understanding.

reviews.rationale: 'Essentially regurgitation', as Marcus glosses it, and 'knows what words mean' have no agreed operational test. The only evidence concerns GPT-2 and literal copying. The claim is too vague to score, so not adjudicable.
